\section{How Brokers Accumulate Informational and Structural Advantage: A Formal Illustration}

\subsection{Model and Methods}

I use an agent-based model (ABM) to formalize the theory and examine its
feedback mechanisms among heterogeneous, boundedly informed actors. The model
is a formal illustration, not a test of the theory. Complete pseudocode and
specifications appear in Appendices A and B. The public Julia repository
(\texttt{https://github.com/m-laprise/brokerage-abm}) contains the code and
scripts needed to reproduce the simulations, statistics, figures, and text.

\emph{Market and matching}. Many principals and one broker occupy an undirected
network (Appendix B \S\S4, 6--7). Each period, principals seek pairwise matches
either through self-search or through the broker. They choose between channels
using satisfaction with past outcomes net of search costs or broker fees. A
completed match creates a direct tie that persists until either party exits;
each principal exits with probability $\eta$ and is replaced by a new entrant.

Each principal has a fixed vector of observable characteristics. Match output
combines general quality, which depends on each party separately, and
complementarity, which depends on how their types interact (Appendix B \S2). The
mixing weight $\rho$ ranges from pure complementarity at $\rho=0$ to pure general
quality at $\rho=1$. The parameter $\delta$ determines how sharply
complementarity changes across a boundary in type-pair space and therefore how
difficult that component is to learn. Because $\delta$ acts only on
complementarity, it has no effect when $\rho=1$.

\emph{Learning and information}. Principals observe their own matches, each
partner's type, and realized output. The broker observes both parties' types and
outcomes for all matches it mediates (Appendix A \S3; Appendix B \S3). Each uses
a small neural network to predict match output. The broker pools observations
across clients and represents both parties symmetrically, whereas each principal
learns only from its own history. Predicted values rank candidates; tied
predictions are ordered uniformly at random. Offers are made to the highest-ranked
candidates whose predicted output exceeds the reservation threshold. Further
search, training, and match-formation details appear in Appendices A and B.

I repeat the complete design with Ridge regression replacing both neural
networks. Principals use candidate characteristics, while the broker uses
symmetric additive and bilinear pair features. Penalties were selected on 10
baseline calibration seeds excluded from reporting (Appendix B \S3). Three
additional Ridge versions isolate the broker's data advantage by limiting its
sample size, retaining only one party's characteristics from each match, or
omitting interactions between the two parties' characteristics.

\emph{Measurement}. Broker betweenness centrality measures the share of shortest
paths between principals that pass through the broker (Brandes 2001; Freeman
1977). The access fraction is the share of brokered matches between principals
who were not already tied. Supplementary Figures S1--S3 reproduce the structural
analyses using Burt's constraint and effective size. Prediction quality is
evaluated on random-partner holdout samples. Spearman rank correlation measures
candidate ordering and reproduces the random ordering of tied predictions.
Holdout $R^2$ measures level accuracy but is diagnostic only. It can become
extremely negative when holdout-output variance is small and never enters a
decision rule (Appendix B \S8).

\emph{Simulation design and analysis}. At the baseline, $N=1{,}000$ principals
interact for $T=500$ periods with $\rho=0.5$, $\delta=0.5$, and $\eta=0.02$.
One-at-a-time changes and eight two-parameter grids vary the matching problem,
turnover, market size, reservation threshold, initial network, broker roster,
and self-search pool (Appendix B \S9). The design contains \pv{nRegimes} unique
regimes after duplicate coordinates and inactive parameters are consolidated.
There are \pv{nGeneralSeeds} independent seeds per regime and
\pv{nBaselineSeeds} at the baseline (\pv{nRuns} runs total).

Reported late levels average periods $t\in[481,500]$ within each seed and then
across seeds; early levels use $t\in[50,70]$. Cross-regime summaries give each
regime equal weight. Time-series figures begin at $t=30$ to omit the
initialization transient, without changing the simulations or estimands. Monte
Carlo convergence was assessed by nested-seed comparisons and Student-$t$ 95\%
intervals. Across the \pv{mcOutcomeCount} non-$R^2$ figure outcomes, median
relative interval half-widths ranged from \pv{mcCiMedianMinPercent}\% to
\pv{mcCiMedianMaxPercent}\%, and median nested-seed changes ranged from
\pv{mcNestedMedianMinPercent}\% to \pv{mcNestedMedianMaxPercent}\%. Regimes whose
interval contains zero are assessed from absolute intervals instead.

\subsection{The Broker Primarily Provides Assessment, Not Access}

Across the tested regimes, the broker is usually the dominant channel in the
market. The outsourcing rate as a share of demand is \pv{outBaselineLate} at the
baseline (late mean, up from an early mean of \pv{outBaselineEarly}) and has a
median of \pv{outBaseMed} across regimes. It exceeds one-half in
\pv{outBaseDominantN} of \pv{nRegimes} regimes; the remaining regimes all have
no turnover. Yet the broker primarily assesses options within the existing
network rather than providing access beyond it. The access fraction (the share of
brokered placements between principals with no pre-existing tie) has a late mean
of \pv{accessAcrossBaseLate} across regimes, down from
\pv{accessAcrossBaseEarly} early, and never exceeds \pv{accessBaseMax}. It
declines over time in all \pv{nRegimes} regimes, with paired 95\% intervals below
zero in all \pv{accessDeclineCIN}. Most brokered matches therefore connect
principals already tied to each other. Figure~\ref{fig:dynamics} and
Table~\ref{tab:baseline-measures} summarize these baseline dynamics and the main
measures.

Widespread broker use is generally, but not always, accompanied by higher realized
output. Mean realized output is higher through the broker channel than through
self-search in \pv{ogapBasePosN} regimes, and the output gap (broker minus
self-search) averages $\pv{ogapBaseMean}$ across regimes (late means). Paired 95\%
Monte Carlo intervals are above zero in
\pv{ogapBaseCIPosN} regimes and below zero in \pv{ogapBaseCINegN}. The negative
gaps occur in \pv{ogapBaseNegN} regimes, all with no or nearly no turnover
($\eta\in\{0,0.001\}$). Broker use and output differ because principals choose a
channel using satisfaction scores that include unfilled requests, fees, and search
costs, whereas the output gap compares realized output among formed matches. The
gap also reflects the candidates considered, offers made, and offers mutually
accepted. Outsourcing is therefore not itself evidence that the broker always
produces better matches.

The broker's assessment advantage appears more consistently in ranking candidates
than in predicting output levels. On a held-out sample of random partners
(Appendix~A~\S8), its rank correlation is \pv{brokerRankBaseline} at the
baseline and has a median of \pv{brokerRankBaseMed} across regimes, compared with
\pv{agentRankBaseline} and \pv{agentRankBaseMed} for principals. The
broker-minus-principal difference in holdout rank correlation is positive in \pv{rankGapNNPosN} of
\pv{nRegimes} regimes. Paired 95\% intervals are above zero in
\pv{rankGapNNCiPosN} regimes and below zero in only \pv{rankGapNNCiNegN}. The two
nonpositive point estimates occur on the hardest pure-complementarity problems
discussed below.
The broker's level accuracy is less consistent, but not uniformly poor: its
holdout $R^2$ is \pv{brokerR2Baseline} at baseline, has a median of
\pv{brokerR2BaseMed} across regimes, and is positive in
\pv{brokerR2PositiveN} of \pv{nRegimes} regimes. Candidate selection requires a
useful ordering, not an accurate prediction of each candidate's absolute output.

Within the model, the broker's core service is choosing among accessible
counterparties, not finding otherwise unreachable ones. Its ranking advantage
appears under pure general quality as well as complementarity: at $\rho=1$, the
broker-minus-principal difference in holdout rank correlation averages \pv{rhoOneRankGapMean} and is positive in
all \pv{rhoOneRankGapPosN} pure-quality regimes.
The one-at-a-time checks also show that initial network degree ($k_G$), broker
roster fraction, and the number of strangers available in self-search have
comparatively small effects on the main economic outcomes.

\subsection{The Broker's Information Advantage Comes from Pooled, Pair-Level Data}

The ordering advantage does not depend on neural-network learning. When Ridge
regression replaces both neural networks, the broker-minus-principal difference in
holdout rank correlation is
\pv{ridgeBaselineGap} at the baseline, has a median of \pv{ridgeMedianGap} across
the \pv{ridgeNConditions} regimes, and is positive in all \pv{ridgePositiveN}.
Supplementary Figure S4 reports the pattern across regimes and the
$\rho\times\delta$ design.
The paired-Ridge broker still has more observations and retains more information
about each pair than a principal. Three additional Ridge experiments impose the
restrictions described above. Because each restriction changes later matching and
learning, their effects need not add up.

Pooled sample size accounts for much of the advantage
(Fig.~\ref{fig:information-sources}). Across the \pv{ablationConditionN} regimes
in the baseline and $\rho\times\delta$ design, the median broker-minus-principal
difference in holdout rank correlation is
\pv{ablationPairMedianGap} under paired Ridge but only
\pv{ablationSizeMedianGap} with a size-matched broker. The size-matched difference remains
positive in \pv{ablationSizePositiveN} of \pv{ablationConditionN} regimes, so
pooling is important without being the broker's only advantage.

The information retained in each observation also matters. When the broker retains
the type of only one party, the median broker-minus-principal difference in
holdout rank correlation is
\pv{ablationSingleMedianGap} and is positive in only
\pv{ablationSinglePositiveN} regimes. When it retains both parties only through
the sum of their types, omitting their interaction, the corresponding figures are
\pv{ablationAdditiveMedianGap} and \pv{ablationAdditivePositiveN}. The cost of
omitting the interaction is greatest when complementarity matters; under pure
general quality, it is unnecessary. The broker's information advantage therefore
comes from both the number of observations it pools and whether each observation
retains information about both parties and their interaction, not from
neural-network flexibility alone.

\subsection{The Nature of the Matching Problem Shapes the Broker's Advantage}
\label{sec:matching-shapes}

Different markets present brokers with matching problems of different kinds. In
this model, $\rho=0$ gives pure complementarity and $\rho=1$ gives pure general
quality. The parameter $\delta$ increases learning difficulty by making
complementarity payoffs change more sharply across a boundary in type-pair space.
At $\rho=1$, complementarity disappears and $\delta$ has no effect. This endpoint
is therefore a separate boundary condition, not a smooth continuation of the
interior $\rho$ values. Broker centrality is governed primarily by the composition
of match value ($\rho$). Betweenness centrality falls
from \pv{betwRho0} at $\rho=0$ to \pv{betwRho1} at $\rho=1$, while the access
fraction rises from \pv{accessRho0} to \pv{accessRho1} (late means along the
one-at-a-time sweep, $\delta=0.5$). The $\rho\times\eta$ grid shows the same
relationship at every turnover rate: moving from $\rho=0$ to $\rho=0.85$ raises
access and lowers centrality.

Difficulty changes the broker's informational advantage only when complementarity
contributes substantially to match value. Under pure complementarity, increasing
$\delta$ from 0 to 1 lowers the broker's rank correlation from
\pv{brokerRankRho0D0} to \pv{brokerRankRho0D1} and changes the
broker-minus-principal difference in holdout rank correlation from
\pv{rankGapRho0D0} to \pv{rankGapRho0D1}
(Fig.~\ref{fig:grid}). This effect fades as $\rho$ approaches general quality and
disappears at $\rho=1$ by construction. Paired 95\% intervals for this difference are
above zero in \pv{gridRankGapCIPosN} of the \pv{rhoDeltaEffectiveN} regimes. Only
the two hardest pure-complementarity conditions depart from the
general pattern: one interval includes zero and the other is below zero. This is a
qualification to the neural-network result, not a general failure of broker
learning. With paired Ridge, this difference remains positive in every regime.

The broker's realized output advantage is greatest when match value depends on
complementarity. Paired 95\% intervals for the broker-minus-self-search output gap
are above zero in all \pv{gridOutputGapCIPosN} regimes, including the two hardest
pure-complementarity conditions. This does not imply that poorer holdout rankings
produce better matches. Holdout rank correlation evaluates random partner sets;
realized channel output also reflects endogenous candidate pools, offers, and
mutual acceptance. The broker's realized-output advantage survives where its
relative NN ranking advantage does not, but the results do not identify which
stage of the matching process accounts for that difference.

\caption{\textbf{\pvtitle{grid}.} \pvcaption{grid}}
\label{fig:grid}
\end{figure}

\subsection{A Broker Can Be Highly Central While Doing Little Bridging}

In most regimes, the broker's structural position strengthens over time while the
principal network thins. At the baseline, mean principal degree falls from
\pv{degBaselineEarly} to \pv{degBaselineLate}, while broker betweenness centrality
rises from \pv{betwBaselineEarly} to \pv{betwBaselineLate} (early to late means).
This co-movement occurs in \pv{comoveN} of \pv{nRegimes} regimes,
and principal degree falls in \pv{degFallsN} of them
(Fig.~\ref{fig:position}). In most regimes, direct ties do not accumulate fast
enough to offset turnover. The broker's structural advantage therefore does not
self-liquidate.

The distinction between assessment and access explains this relationship. An
access match creates a direct tie between previously unconnected principals and
can remove the broker from their shortest path. An assessment match reuses an
existing tie, so the broker can serve the market without directly densifying the
principal network.
This explains why complementarity-heavy matching can sustain high broker
centrality while most brokered matches reuse existing ties. Figure~\ref{fig:position}
isolates a distinct turnover effect. Holding $\rho$ fixed, increasing turnover
raises access and centrality at every tested $\rho$. The access fraction therefore
has no uniform association with centrality. Turnover creates network gaps;
matching composition determines how often brokerage closes them with direct ties.

The turnover effect is substantial but nonlinear. Holding other parameters at
baseline, increasing $\eta$ from 0 to 0.03 lowers late mean principal degree from
\pv{degEta0Late} to \pv{degEta003Late} and raises broker centrality from
\pv{betwEta0Late} to \pv{betwEta003Late}, with most of the change occurring between
$\eta=0.001$ and $0.01$. Turnover also changes realized broker value. In the
$\rho\times\eta$ grid, the 95\% interval for the broker-minus-self-search output
gap is below zero in \pv{qgapEta0CINegN} of \pv{rhoEtaRhoN} $\rho$ conditions at
$\eta=0$, but above zero in \pv{qgapEta01CIPosN} of \pv{rhoEtaRhoN} by
$\eta=0.01$. In the model, turnover supplies both structural opportunities and the
conditions under which brokered matches outperform self-search.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figs/fig3_position_work.png}
\caption{\textbf{\pvtitle{position}.} \pvcaption{position}}
\label{fig:position}
\end{figure}

The pure-quality boundary confirms that low access alone is not sufficient for high
centrality. Although higher turnover raises centrality there, centrality remains
below pure complementarity at the same turnover rate. In the tested regimes, high
centrality occurs when turnover renews network gaps and brokerage mainly assesses
existing relationships. Because access remains low overall and declines within
runs, brokerage does little to eliminate the structural basis of its own position.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth]{figs/fig4_advantage.png}
\caption{\textbf{\pvtitle{advantage}.} \pvcaption{advantage}}
\label{fig:advantage}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:advantage} shows that structural position relates differently to
relative ranking and realized value. Across otherwise matched parameter settings,
moving from pure complementarity to pure general quality reduces the output gap from
\pv{ogapRho0Group} to \pv{ogapRho1Group}, while increasing the
broker-minus-principal difference in holdout rank correlation from
\pv{rankGapRho0Group} to
\pv{rankGapRho1Group}. The broker is therefore most central and produces its
largest realized-output advantage where its relative holdout-ranking advantage is
smaller. Taken together, the results separate the sources of informational,
economic, and structural advantage: pooled pair-level data improves ranking,
complementarity raises broker value, and turnover renews the network gaps that
sustain centrality. These advantages need not move together.

\subsection{Propositions}

The simulation results motivate the following falsifiable propositions for
future empirical research. These propositions extend the model's implications
beyond the simulated setting:

\noindent\textbf{P1.} In complex matching markets, brokers add value primarily by
assessing reachable counterparties rather than by bridging disconnected parties;
this advantage is greater when match quality depends more heavily on
complementarity.

\noindent\textbf{P2.} A broker's betweenness centrality is produced by outsourcing
volume and client satisfaction, it tracks how much complementarity matters to match
value, and assessment-heavy brokers tend to retain or gain centrality as networks
evolve.

\noindent\textbf{P3.} Holding market turnover constant, bridging position and
bridging behavior are negatively related: assessment-heavy brokers tend to be
more central while doing less bridging. Higher turnover can raise both access
and centrality by continually creating new network gaps.

\noindent\textbf{P4.} Broker predictive advantage tracks the complexity of learning
the complementarities relevant to match value, and it can diverge from structural
centrality.
